title: Technics EAH-A1000 kulaklık manyetik sıvı sürücülerle duyuruldu
summary: Technics, ses bozulmasını azaltmak için manyetik sıvı sürücüler kullanan yeni amiral gemisi kablosuz kulak üstü kulaklığı EAH-A1000 modelini tanıttı.
body:
Technics, ses bozulmasını azaltmak ve geniş bir ses alanı sunmak amacıyla manyetik sıvı teknolojisini kullanan yeni amiral gemisi kablosuz kulak üstü kulaklığı **Technics EAH-A1000** modelini duyurdu. Panasonic'e bağlı markanın kulak üstü kategorisinde ilk kez kullandığı bu özel sıvı teknoloji, ses bobini ile sürücü mıknatısı arasında yer alarak hassas hareketi destekliyor ve istenmeyen titreşimleri en aza indiriyor.

## Öne çıkan teknik özellikler

Kulaklıklar, düşük ağırlığı ve rijitliği nedeniyle tercih edilen karbon fiberden üretilen 40 mm'lik özel sürücülere sahip. Bunun yanı sıra, markanın hoparlör ürünlerinden uyarlanan Symmetrical Surround Technology (SST) kenar tasarımı ve hareketli parçaların arkasında yer alan bir akustik kontrol odası hava akışını optimize ediyor. Kulaklık, Hi-Res LDAC codec desteğinin yanı sıra USB-C üzerinden kayıpsız oynatma ve kafa takipli Dolby Atmos uzaysal ses özelliklerini barındırıyor. Aynı anda üç cihaza kadar çoklu nokta bağlantısı kurabilen cihaz, ANC (aktif gürültü engelleme) açıkken kablosuz kullanımda yaklaşık 40 saat pil ömrü sunarken, ANC kapalıyken bu süre 80 ila 90 saate kadar çıkabiliyor. Ancak Engadget'ın aktardığına göre bazı basın bültenlerinde pil süresinin ANC kullanımı detaylandırılmaksızın 45 saate kadar ulaşabileceği de belirtiliyor.

## Fiyat ve çıkış tarihi

T3 ve Stuff kaynaklarının aktardığı bilgilere göre Technics EAH-A1000, Avrupa'da 449 euro, İngiltere'de ise 399 sterlin fiyat etiketiyle 30 Eylül'de satışa çıkıyor. ABD fiyatı ve küresel pazarın tamamındaki fiyatlandırma ise henüz netlik kazanmadı. Siyah ve gri-platin tonlarındaki "greige" renk seçenekleriyle gelen kulaklıklar, Sony WH-1000XM6 ve Bowers & Wilkins PX7 S3 gibi modellere rakip olarak konumlandırılıyor.

**Neden önemli?** Kulaklık pazarındaki rekabet kızışırken, Technics'in ses bozulmasını en aza indirmek için in-ear modellerinden uyarladığı manyetik sıvı teknolojisini ilk kez kulak üstü formata taşımaları ses meraklıları için yeni bir alternatif yaratıyor.

source_texts.title: Technics’ latest over-ear headphones use liquid for distortion-free sound- here’s how
source_texts.summary: The Technics EAH-A1000 are right up against other key headphones such as Sony’s WH-1000XM6. And from my early listening they certainly match up to their rivals
source_texts.text:
Technics has debuted a wireless noise-cancelling headphone that’s designed to go up against the big players, with its $449/£399/€449 price point putting the EAH-A1000 over-ears right up against other key headphones such as Sony’s WH-1000XM6 and Bowers & Wilkins PX7 S3.
And it doesn’t just match them on price – from my early listening they match on sound quality as well. I’ll be bringing you a full Technics EAH-A1000 review soon, but Technics has released some recent firmware updates for the transparency mode and noise-cancelling and I’m testing that out currently.
The headphones are available in black and what Panasonic-owned Technics calls ‘greige’. I’d never heard of it, but the color has a bit of a heritage. It is basically grey/platinum though, matching the similar color from other vendors such as Sony and Sonos. Technics has put a lot of work into the design of these headphones, with a so-called ‘flow arm’ design. They are very comfortable but are quite chunky as you can see, which might not appeal to all would-be purchasers.
Key to the new headphones’ sound quality is its latest-gen 40mm Magnetic Fluid driver which actually does contain a small amount of especially developed fluid, previously used by the brand in its EAH-TZ700 and EAH-AZ100 in-ear headphones. One of the key ideas was to remove distortion but bring as large a soundstage as possible.
The headphones do support Hi-Res LDAC as well as lossless playback via USB-C while they also have head-tracked Dolby Atmos spatial audio, too. And they can support up to three devices paired at the same time with near-seamless switching.
They have some excellent physical controls rather than relying on ear-cup touch controls like several key rivals. Battery life is around 40 hours when listening wirelessly at high quality with noise-cancelling (ANC) on, but you if you’ve got ANC off they can stretch to an incredible 80-90 hours.
At a recent launch event in Tokyo I learned more about Technics approach to these headphones. “Simply creating a larger version of our existing driver was not enough. We wanted to create an over-ear listening experience that only technology could deliver.
“So we brought together the technologies and expertise we have developed across personal audio and hi-fi. We brought together everything we have learned from decades of sound engineering and our experience in personal audio. We challenged ourselves to create an overall platform that delivers not only remarkable sound, but the complete listening experience worthy of the Technics name.”

source_texts.title: Technics EAH-A1000 review: Distinctive headphones bring 5-star sound
source_texts.summary: With unique technologies, Technics has delivered a flagship that's a big statement in a niche all of its own
source_texts.text:
The Technics EAH-A1000 bring big sound and presentation, thanks to unique audio technologies working behind the scenes. Big is the operative word, though, as such tech does mean the A1000's earcups protrude more than your average – and some people will find that a deterrent. While the A1000 won't be for everyone, therefore, their niche nature and distinctive design bring strong appeals of their own. But it's the sound and active noise-cancelling (ANC) that'll keep you coming back for more – time and time again.
- 
+Incredible sound that'll serve myriad genres – showing off Technics' known versatility
- 
+Impressive active noise-cancelling (ANC) with always-listening Adaptive mode
- 
+Solid 40-hour battery life (with best LDAC quality)
- 
-The nature of design means earcups protrude significantly from the head
- 
-Control buttons a little plasticky – Sonos delivers better aesthetic
- 
-Not short of competition at this price point
Why you can trust T3
Technics has pulled off some blinders in recent years when it comes to in-ear and over-ear audio. The EAH-A800 over-ears from four-and-a-bit years ago were a 5-star wonder, as was the impressive (and award-winning) EAH-AZ100 in-ears released just last year.
Looking to trump both those products, however, is this: the all-new EAH-A1000 over-ears, which deploy updated unique technologies taken from both the AZ100 and the brand's storied speaker products. The goal is for a high-end, high-resolution pair of headphones that stand apart from their peers.
But standing apart is ever more difficult in a market bustling with choice: from Sonos' just-released Ace Ultra and their ecosystem-targeted Wi-Fi functionality; to Bowers & Wilkins' PX7 S3 and their luxury design and material choices; to Sony's WH-1000XM6 for the ultimate in travel headphones and noise-cancelling (ANC) capabilities.
Technics hasn't explicitly tried to take on any one of those examples head-on, mind, carving out a niche of its own by doubling down on its technologies and sound quality in a design that may position them as home-listening headphones for many. Yet their lightweight nature – despite large-scale physicality – and ANC credits mean they're also versatile enough to use while on the go.
Price & Availability
The Technics EAH-A1000 are available now (from 30 September), with a launch price set at £399 in the UK and €449 in Europe. They will go on sale worldwide, but US and wider regional pricing is yet to be determined at the time of writing.
That positions the A1000 at £/€100 more than the earlier (and less advanced) A800 model, so by that logic the US asking price for the A1000 could be $549 – but we'll have to wait and see, given current market complications.
What's New?
While I've mentioned the previous A800 model, I won't really be discussing those headphones from here on – as the A1000 is an entirely different product with a heap of its own innovation. Indeed, there are some core aspects in the A1000 that provide a unique edge.
Get all the latest news, reviews, deals and buying guides on gorgeous tech, home and active products from the T3 experts
The first is the brand's Magnetic Fluid Driver technology, which uses a magnetic oil-like liquid that sits between voice coil and driver magnet, to support precise movement and suppress unwanted vibrations and distortion. This has been adapted from the AZ100 in-ears, but it needed lots of tweaking to make it possible at this larger scale.
The second is the custom dome-and-cone-shaped 40mm driver, which is made from carbon fibre – selected due to its low weight and inherent rigidity. However, Technics pulled upon its SST Edge technology (that's 'Symmetrical Surround Technology'), derived from some of its established speaker products, to ensure airflow during movement remained symmetrical.
Being able to produce a carbon fibre diaphragm to the specified shape proved tricky, though, as the material's hardness caused challenges with moulding and deformation. Technics worked around this by weaving fibre directions and adding a physical 'rib' to the dome to provide stability. No compromise to shape, nor on the material choice.
An Acoustic Control Chamber behind the driver helps manage airflow, minimise irregularities, and drive the acoustic path to the ear with utmost clarity. This, combined with the above technologies, gives the A1000 its unique sonic properties. But such technologies are also what makes the earcups protrude more than you average – as there's so much to accommodate within.
Design
How you feel about that physical size could be the deciding factor in whether these are the headphones for you, as this is no slim-profile, Sonos-style product. I've felt conscious of that when wearing these headphones for travel, not that it's as eye-catching a prospect as something zany, like Nothing's Headphone (1).
That said, there's nothing heavy about the A1000 headphones. The 306g weight is roughly that of, say, Bowers & Wilkins PX7 S3, and the way the Technics headphones position over the head feels balanced, comfortable and avoids any undue clamping force – with the headband effortlessly (and silently) adjustable.
There's been a lot of thought in what Technics calls its Flow Arm structure – the arms which hold the earcups to the headband. It flows from a square structure to a triangular one at its end, giving this a fluid visual. However, I do wish as much attention was paid to some surrounding details, as the visual presence of a hex-screwhead and notable openings for the folding mechanics don't look quite as refined.
Technics has opted for physical controls here, too, with two buttons flanking a toggle control on the right earcup. They're easy to reach, making pairing, skipping tracks and adjusting volume a breeze, although the look and feel – when inspected up close – isn't to the same lofty heights as Sonos' latest Ace Ultra headphones in my view. It, too, could be further finessed.
I'm also not a fan of the Platinum Greige name – per my review photographs – but do think the visual appeal is undeniable. Especially those metal earcaps, which are aluminium and finished with a spun-blasted technique for a distinct look in the way light catches in them. The Technics logo looks grand in gold, just as it does on the alternative Black finish option.
Sound & ANC
When I was first introduced to the A1000, the listening sessions Technics presented to me were largely built around instrumental jazz records, which the headphones presented very well – bar some minor resonance when wired USB-C listening at higher volumes.
Since then, I've explored all kinds of music with the A1000 and the myriad genres it rewards is reflective of Technics' versatility. That's an echo of how the brand is represented, from its roots in classical jazz through to DMC scratch DJ competitions.

source_texts.text:
Technics brings magnetic fluid drivers to new EAH-A1000 headphones
The tech should reduce audio distortion for these over-ear ANC cans.
Technics has released the next generation of its flagship over-ear adaptive noise cancelling headphones with a new focus on low-distortion audio. The Panasonic-owned brand unveiled the EAH-A1000, which feature 40 mm magnetic fluid drivers. It's the brand's first use of the magnetic fluid tech in an over-ear headphone model. The drivers allow for movement while reducing the vibrations and distortions that can accompany large drivers. The EAH-A1000 also minimizes distortion by using a surround sound technology, or SST, edge like the ones found in some of Technics' speakers.
The ANC tech for this headset comes thanks to three feed-forward microphones and one feedback microphone on each side. The arrangement is meant to optimize noise-cancellation based on both the fit of the headphones and the ambient noise while they're in use.
These headphones support the LDAC codec as well as lossless listening via USB Audio. It's an unusual instance of multipoint connectivity across up to three devices rather than the usual two. Technics' press release says the EAH-A1000 can reach a battery life of up to 45 hours of continuous playback, but did not specify how much of that included ANC use, which creates a bigger power drain than passive listening. The company also hasn't shared any specifics yet regarding price or availability for this new flagship model.
